gap: No result ChatGPT got says that USB-C KVM docks keep the MacBook below 4K 144 Hz. On AV Access's own pages, the iDock B10 gives its USB-C laptop input '4K@120Hz' while its HDMI 2.1 and DP inputs reach 4K@165Hz, and the Mac-specific iDock M10 is listed only at '4K@60Hz'.
standout_why: I compared against three pages. The cited Level1Techs single-monitor store page gives only its own 4K120 limit. The top uncited guide, dockgearhq 'Best 4K KVM Switches (2026)', names ten KVMs, has no prices and covers no USB-C-dock Mac input limit; it doesn't name AV Access at all. ChatGPT's own answer says only that a USB-C docking KVM 'isn't necessarily capable of 4K 144Hz', with no model or figure. I could not open the cited TESmart blog pages today (HTTP 429), but they cover TESmart's own HDMI 2.1 and DP products, which have no USB-C input.
decides: It confirms that our two listed KVMs, the AV Access iDock M10 and KD-E10, are wrong for this question. The M10 tops out at 4K60, and the KD-E10 is 4K60 as well, because AV Access says it is functionally the same as the C10. It also rules out the 'Mac on USB-C dock' setup in general: even AV Access's best dock, the B10, holds the Mac to 4K120. The pick stays a DisplayPort path for both computers: the MacBook on a USB-C-to-DP cable into a DP 1.4 KVM, or straight into the monitor's own input or built-in KVM. The Level1Techs single-monitor 2-computer KVM is officially 4K120 and sold out today. So the page's main advice, 'use the monitor's KVM', still stands.
